argument: The episode redefines superstition broadly as falsely attributing an effect to a cause, and shows this pattern runs through everyday beliefs about happiness, sports rituals, and old maritime customs, not just obviously silly ideas. Berkeley targets a deeper superstition: the unexamined assumption that some independently existing material reality causes our perceptions, when all we ever actually experience is the perception itself; since he was worried that a self-sustaining material substance could let God be reasoned out of the universe, he concludes only minds and ideas exist, with God's perpetual perception keeping everything in existence. Voltaire, meanwhile, attacks superstition and intolerance in religion itself, using his observations of England's religiously diverse marketplace in Letters Concerning the English Nation to argue that many competing faiths, not one or two dominant ones, produce social peace.
keyIdeas: Superstition, in the episode's dictionary-style definition, is falsely attributing an effect to a cause, a pattern that shows up in mundane beliefs about wealth and happiness just as much as in old sailors' rituals.

Berkeley's key move is questioning the assumption that some independent material reality exists behind our perceptions, since empiricism holds all knowledge comes from sense experience and we never actually experience that supposed underlying matter.

Berkeley worried that treating matter as a self-sustaining substance would let God become unnecessary to daily reality, so he concludes only minds exist, with God's perpetual perception keeping the world (including an unwatched falling tree) in existence.
Voltaire's anti-Semitism was unusual for his era: rather than blaming Jews for killing Jesus, he resented them for making Christianity, one of his primary targets, possible in the first place.

In Letters Concerning the English Nation, Voltaire observed that England's marketplace, with many coexisting religions, was more peaceful than a system with only one or two, since many competitors prevents any single religion from dominating or feeling threatened.
